title: Lazarus (John 11:1–44)
hookLine: four days in the tomb, Martha's faith, and the shortest verse, Jesus wept

lines: HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.
cards: A message arrives from two sisters we've met, Martha and Mary, in the village of Bethany. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." That's all it says.
Their brother Lazarus, his friend. Jesus, John tells us, loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. And then he waits two more days before he goes.
By the time he gets to Bethany, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. The house is full of mourners. Martha hears he's coming and goes out to meet him on the road.
She doesn't say hello. She says what anyone would say.

teach.b: Martha says: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Grief and faith in one breath.

teach.h: I AM THE RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE.
teach.b: Jesus answers: "I am the resurrection and the life." Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live. Do you believe this?
And Martha, the busy sister from the kitchen, makes a bold statement of faith: Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.

Then Mary comes, falls at his feet, and says the very same words: Lord, if you had been here. She's weeping, the mourners with her are weeping, and Jesus, John says, is deeply moved and troubled. Where have you laid him?
And then: "And Jesus wept." A whole verse, three words; in Greek, too. John uses a different verb from the mourners' weeping: not wailing, but tears running down.
He knows he's about to call Lazarus out. And he weeps anyway. Christians read in this that God doesn't skip past grief, even when the ending is already known.
The people watching say: see how he loved him. At the tomb, Martha, practical to the end, warns him: Lord, by now there'll be a smell, it's been four days. They roll the stone away.
Jesus prays, and cries with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still wrapped in grave clothes.
Unbind him, Jesus says, and let him go. This week: loaves, the water, the mountain, two sisters, a tree, the stones, and now a tomb.

how: Catholics hear the raising of Lazarus on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year A, and John 11 is one of the Gospels often chosen for funeral Masses, with its words, I am the resurrection and the life.

games.q: you're Martha. your brother died four days ago, and Jesus has finally come. you go out to meet him on the road. what do you say?
o: if you had been here, my brother wouldn't have died.
it's too late now. go home.
games.why: “Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” and then she says she believes he is the Christ.

practice: Is there a loss you haven't let yourself feel: a person, a friendship, a version of your life that didn't happen, maybe because you've been too busy or thought you should be over it?
Let it come gently, without explaining or fixing it, and if tears come, let them; he wept too. If you pray, you can tell God what Martha told him: if you had been here.

wordCard.voice: Lazarus. The friend Jesus wept for, and then called out of the tomb after four days. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he shed tears, he wept quietly. A different verb from the loud wailing of the mourners.
